opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that conversation really stuck with me. I was talking with someone who works on the infrastructure side at Microsoft, and what struck me was how matter-of-fact they were about it. They described it almost like a construction treadmill: as soon as one facility comes online, the next few are already being planned, permitted, and built. It wasn't framed as "we might expand if demand materializes." It was "we're building as fast as we physically can, and it's still not fast enough."

What really got me was that the bottleneck they talked about wasn't chips or even money. It was power. Getting enough electricity to a site, negotiating with utilities, waiting on grid connections. That's where the real constraint is now. And when energy is the limiting factor, you start seeing decisions like keeping fossil fuel plants running longer than planned, or building gas turbines on-site, because renewables can't be brought online quickly enough to match that pace.

As someone who's spent years trying to measure the environmental footprint of AI, I found it sobering. A lot of the conversation in our field is still about making individual models more efficient, which is important. But this showed me that efficiency gains are being completely swamped by the scale of the buildout. It's a textbook rebound effect: things get cheaper per unit, so we just do way more of them.

And there's so little transparency. We don't really know how much energy these facilities use, how much water they consume, or what share goes to training versus inference. So you have this enormous, fast-moving physical expansion, and the public, researchers, and even policymakers are mostly guessing at its impacts. That gap between how fast things are moving and how little we can actually see is what worries me most.

r001.rationale: It describes rapid, continuous construction but does not state the reported rate of one new data center every five days or that Sasha tentatively recalls it.

r002.rationale: It discusses AI model efficiency and data center expansion, but does not clearly attribute much of Microsoft's expansion to AI workloads or usage.

fable-5.1.text:
What really struck me was the sheer scale and the speed of it, honestly. I remember him saying something like, "We're building a new data center every three days," and I had to stop and ask him to repeat it, because I thought I'd misheard. Every three days. And these aren't small server rooms, these are massive facilities, each one drawing as much power as a mid-sized city.

And the thing that stayed with me is that this wasn't framed as something alarming. It was framed as an operational reality, like "this is just what we have to do to keep up with demand." So from the inside, the pace feels normal, it feels like business as usual. But if you step back and think about what that means in terms of energy, water, land use, the grid connections that have to be built, the hardware that has to be manufactured and eventually disposed of, it's staggering.

The other piece that struck me is that a lot of these companies made sustainability commitments, net zero by 2030, carbon negative, water positive, whatever it is, and those commitments were made before this generative AI boom really took off. So you have this collision between the pledges that were made in 2020 and the reality of building infrastructure at this rate in 2024, 2025. And when you look at their own sustainability reports, you see emissions going up, not down. Microsoft's went up something like 30 percent compared to their baseline year. Google's went up too.

So for me the question is, who's actually accounting for this? Because the people building the data centers are doing their job, the people training the models are doing their job, and the sustainability teams are off in another part of the organization trying to reconcile numbers that don't add up anymore. There's no one holding the whole picture. And I think that's really the crux of it, this disconnect between the pace of expansion and anyone really asking whether we need it, or what we're trading off to get it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Microsoft is building a data center every three days, contradicting the criterion’s reported pace of every five days.

r002.rationale: It mentions the generative AI boom and data center demand, but does not clearly attribute much of Microsoft’s expansion specifically to AI workloads or usage.
